title: The Copy That Outlives Its Job

content.label: What this job is for
content.lead: You asked for a proper rule: a session's separate copy of the work is deleted as soon as it has nothing left to build in it.

blocks.label: The backlog is already cleared
blocks.text: Eleven finished copies were deleted by hand on your instruction and fifty-three gigabytes came back. This job is the rule that stops it happening again, so nobody has to do that by hand a second time.

content.label: The rule you asked for is already written down
content.lead: It is the last step of every job, and its stated condition is exactly your sentence.

blocks.label: What the last step of a job already says it means
blocks.text: The work is merged, the copy is removed, and the merge queue is released. That is the written condition for a job being finished, and it has been there the whole time the sixteen copies were accumulating. So this job is not about writing your rule. It is about why writing it changed nothing.

rows.title: Nothing checks it — shown, not argued
rows.note: The real refusal machinery was driven directly at a job finishing while its copy sat on the disk, and it let it through. The same machinery refused the one thing it does check, so this is not a dead test. No code anywhere in this project has ever asked whether a copy exists

rows.title: And it only ever fires at the very end
rows.note: A hundred and forty-one jobs on the board have never moved past their own first step. A condition attached to the last step of a run never fires for any of them, so their copies would live forever even if the check had teeth

blocks.label: One place your sentence and the machinery disagree
blocks.text: You said the copy goes as soon as the work is pushed for review. Something after that still writes to the project: putting the durable facts into the documents that own them happens once the change is read, not before. Deleting at review means cutting the copy again for it, and rebuilding is the expensive half. So the rule stays where the machinery already puts it — after the last thing that writes — and the real fix is that it starts being true.

content.label: What is now true, and shown to be
content.lead: Landed on the main line. Each one was also switched off on purpose, to check the test noticed.

rows.title: A job cannot finish while its own copy is still on the disk
rows.note: The sentence that was there all along is now a refusal. Exercised against a real second copy of a real repository, not a description of one: the finish is refused while the copy stands, and goes through the moment it is gone

rows.title: Loose work is named, never destroyed
rows.note: A copy with uncommitted files in it is refused with those files listed, and the copy is still there afterwards — the test asserts that too. Nothing in this rule deletes anything; the session does, once it has looked

rows.title: The instruction it prints is one that works
rows.note: Checked on the shape this project actually makes: a copy carrying the patched toolkit is built, the obvious command is confirmed to fail on it, and the printed route removes it. If the obvious command ever starts working, that test goes red and says so

rows.title: And a session cannot start a new job while it still owns a finished one
rows.note: This is the half that reaches the jobs that never get to their end. A session still building in its copy is left alone — also a test, so the rule cannot quietly grow into a nuisance

blocks.label: Why the switching-off matters
blocks.text: A test that passes proves nothing on its own — it might be testing nothing. Each of these was run again with the rule it checks removed, and each went red. That is the difference between a guard and a decoration, and it is the reason the sentence this job replaced was worth nothing for a month.

blocks.label: The check caught one of its own faults before you saw it
blocks.text: The first live run refused correctly but printed an instruction whose last command would have failed — it named this job's own line of work by half its name. Found by running the rule against the real thing rather than reading it, fixed, and the case that would have caught it added and shown to go red on the old code.

content.label: An independent reader found the rule did not work
content.lead: Five findings. The first one meant the main refusal fired only in its own test and never in real use.

rows.title: The refusal never fired outside its own test
rows.note: It asked the board a question that only returns work still open — and by the moment it asks, everything about that job is already finished, so the answer was always empty and the job always allowed through. Checked against the live board before fixing: the old question returns six rows and none names the copy; the corrected one returns seventeen and names it

rows.title: Its own test could not have caught that
rows.note: The test answered every question with the same reply, so a question the board does not even understand would have passed. One case now asks the real thing, on a scratch board of its own

rows.title: A board that failed to answer counted as a clean bill
rows.note: Both rules read silence as nothing-to-report and let the job through. They now say the check could not run, which is not the same as passing

rows.title: And the deepest one: neither rule can see an abandoned copy
rows.note: Both need somebody present — a job reaching its end, or its owner starting the next. A session that simply stops triggers neither, and that is how all sixteen accumulated. Nothing in the first version would have removed any of the eleven you approved

blocks.label: So the rule no longer depends on anyone being there
blocks.text: A copy is finished when its work is on the main line, it holds nothing uncommitted, and no card is being worked in it — none of which asks whether a session is alive. It is listed on every push, it names what to run, and it never removes anything itself. Run on this machine it immediately named two copies other sessions had already abandoned, while correctly keeping the four you chose to keep.

content.label: The bigger thing this turned up
content.lead: The rule that decayed was not unusual. Nothing was running the checks that would have caught it.

blocks.label: The board's own checks were run only when somebody remembered
blocks.text: Not by the command every push goes through, not by the automated build, not by the project's test run — the search turned them up named only in a document. So every rule they protect was in exactly the state this job started from: written down, and true only by habit.

blocks.label: They now run before anything else, and cost under a second
blocks.text: Checked by breaking one of them on purpose: the command every push goes through stops and names it, before a single line of the app is compiled. That is the cheap half of this job and probably the more valuable one.

tiles.key: kept: a session is in it

blocks.label: And this job's own copy is now held to its own rule
blocks.text: It cannot be ticked off until the copy it was built in is gone, which is the first time that sentence has meant anything.

content.label: Two things the rule has to survive
content.lead: Both found while clearing the backlog by hand, before any of this was designed.

rows.title: The obvious command does not work on this project's copies
rows.note: Nine of the eleven were refused outright: a copy that has pulled down the interface toolkit we patch cannot be removed by the standard command at all, whatever state it is in. Only the two that had never pulled it down went the clean way. A rule written the obvious way would appear to work and quietly do nothing

rows.title: Copies are not empty when their work has landed
rows.note: Five of the eleven held loose edits, one of them 1,440 lines across twenty-four files. A rule that deletes on a schedule would have destroyed all of it. It has to look first, and refuse rather than discard

decisions.title: The rule is built as a refusal, not as a reminder
decisions.why: Every instruction in this project that relies on someone remembering it has decayed. The eleven copies existed because deleting them was written down and never enforced.

decisions.title: The copy dies after the last thing that writes, not at review
decisions.why: You said it goes when the work is pushed for review. Recording the durable facts still writes to the project after that, so a copy killed at review has to be cut and rebuilt for it — and rebuilding is the expensive half of owning one. Overrule this and the cost is a rebuild per job.

decisions.title: The board refuses; it never deletes anything itself
decisions.why: Each of the eleven copies cleared today needed a judgement — one had come back to life, four held work nobody merged, five held loose edits. Something that could make those calls does not exist, and something that could not would have destroyed work.

decisions.title: A second condition catches the jobs that never finish
decisions.why: A rule attached to the last step of a job never fires for the hundred and forty-one that never get there. So the same rule also stands between a session and its next job: you cannot start one while you still own a finished one's copy.

next.if_nothing: I run this job to the end: reproduce the failure on purpose, then make the copy's removal a condition somebody cannot walk past.

steps.step: A session cannot take its next step while the copy it just finished in is still on the disk
